title: My PIP worked. My job still didn’t
description:
The day I got put on my performance improvement plan (or PIP) in my content marketing job, I drove back to an Appalachian folk magic store I’d happened into the weekend prior. I bought a bottle of Boss Fix Oil, a “conjuring oil” touted as a way of “improving work dynamics.”

I’m not a particularly spiritual man, but I truly was at my wit’s end. I’d been in this role for nearly a year, and in my 25 years of working, I’d never struggled this badly to prove my professional worth. 

A little Googling—and texts from friends—produced the same verdict: PIPs mean they’re trying to get rid of you. Start looking for new employment. 

Needless to say, I was freaking out. But I buckled down, kept my confidence and worked hard through the PIP—and yet? There was something that was bothering me beyond just the PIP. 

Getting put on one made me accept something I was struggling to: the fact that I simply didn’t fit into the culture there.

The “Culture Fit” of It All

The term “culture fit” is divisive in corporate spaces, and understandably so: It introduces subjectivity into a world that likes to pretend it’s a meritocracy. But I also think you can’t overstate the importance of fit in the workplace. A 2023 research review found organizational fit has a much stronger relationship with job satisfaction than job performance. 

The workplace is many things. Objective isn’t always one of them.

I suspected pretty early on that the way I worked and the way this company worked didn’t align. I remember talking to my mother after attending an in-person department summit for the first time. “Everyone was nice enough,” I told her. “But I feel like we approach things very differently.”

I’d tried to get most of my work done ahead of the summit so that, during our downtime, I could participate in the kind of small talk Zoom calls and Slack just don’t facilitate. But during those times? Heads were down, dutifully typing away, and conversations stuck to strategy. Even at our team happy hour, the conversations kept coming back to work projects. My perception? It felt performative—a contest to see who was most devoted.

There were other traits I didn’t fully align with. It was a workplace where climbing the corporate ladder sometimes seemed to take precedence, and navigating office politics seemed more prudent than simply doing good work.

But the big differentiator—and what I suspect ultimately led to my PIP—was what details mattered most. I’m a bigger-picture guy, more concerned with a piece of content’s angle, takeaway, and value to its audience than whether it uses curly or straight quotation marks (something that was apparently important at this job). 

By the time I was put on the PIP, I spent less time thinking strategically and more time stressed about whether an em dash or a semicolon would warrant another talk with my manager about “attention to detail.”

But I didn’t leave. I stayed and worked through the PIP. After all, I’d been laid off a year earlier and had blown through my savings; this new job was a big pay increase I convinced myself I needed. 

But I also wanted to prove I could succeed. I wanted to show I was the kind of guy who could work in tough environments. I think that’s part of why I became so determined to beat the PIP.  

Corporate culture lionizes the person who can “work with anyone,” “thrive in any environment,” and “adapt to changing priorities.” “Agility” and “flexibility” are worn as badges of honor. I’d internalized that. Being good at my job meant being malleable. 

And, frankly, I’d failed at one of the most important aspects of any job: reading the room. I knew my approach differed from the company’s, yet I’d been overconfident in my own. Leaving felt like admitting I couldn’t hack it.

Success Is Subjective 

The easier piece to write—and frankly, the piece my id still wants to—positions me as the victim of the dreaded toxic workplace, the aggrieved creative just trying to do good work somewhere that prized a degree of precision I sometimes found superfluous. But I’ve been deliberately using qualifiers like “my perception” and “estimation” because one person’s toxic could be another person’s ideal.

At a job that was a great fit for me, I remember turning in my first piece of writing and apologizing when a member of upper management had to fix a few typos. 

And yet? “We all make typos,” she told me. “If all I have to do is clean up a few small ones, but the stories are good? You’re excelling.” Plus, at that company’s in-person summit, she started a happy-hour conversation with, “No work talk.” 

That was my favorite job. And it’s 100% the toxic job in someone else’s story: While I liked its informal, collaborative, and relatively unstructured environment (we worked from home and had a lot of freedom in setting our own schedules), there were colleagues—people who thrived with more structure or preferred more hierarchical, competitive environments—who weren’t a good fit.

I don’t believe in magic. I do believe in reframing your thinking. 

So when I Googled ways to optimize conjuring oil use back at the job that served me the PIP, I found a Reddit comment that advised using it with an open mind. It reminded me of another comment I’d found (I’m paraphrasing) during my earlier PIP Googling: “PIPs often aren’t about the quality of your work. They’re about you not fitting in.”

Whether or not that’s the most common truth behind PIPs, I did something I probably should’ve done earlier. I swallowed my pride. It didn’t matter if I thought fixating on quotation marks or putting on a show of productivity was ridiculous. It mattered that this workplace valued it.

Beating the PIP

So, I made myself malleable. And a week into my four-week PIP, things already felt like they were turning around: I focused on the small details. I executed new initiatives without question. I thanked my manager profusely for sharpening my editorial eye and made sure to talk about my “working lunches.”

I passed my PIP with flying colors. 

The month afterward was probably the most aligned I felt with the company since coming on board. I felt like I was making real contributions. I felt like I fit in. 

Was I happy and thriving? I wouldn’t say that. I was the one performing now. And I don’t know—for me, at least—how sustainable that would’ve been. 

I never got to find out.

A month after passing my PIP, en route to an outdoor weekend in Shenandoah National Park for a friend’s 40th—and what felt, a bit, like a victory lap after a stressful Q3—I got a text asking me to check my email and log into a Zoom call about “structural changes that are impacting your role at the organization.” I was laid off in the waiting area of a Virginia rest stop.

My department head assured me it had nothing to do with my performance. Everyone had been very impressed with my recent efforts. This was a business decision. Nothing more.

I believe them. Not only because they wrote me a glowing letter of recommendation, but because I know I’m good at content marketing. Just maybe not . . . there. I also know now that there’s no magic cure for a bad fit. After all, a 2026 survey found that 62% of workers said adopting a professional persona helped their careers, but 65% said doing so drained their energy or motivation.

I think that’s what surprised me most about the whole experience. The PIP worked. I changed the ways I was approaching my job, figured out what was expected of me, and proved I could deliver. 

Even if I disagreed with what this workplace valued, I still had something to learn from it. In fact, I’ve carried some of those lessons into my current job, where I’m noticeably more attentive to details that old me would’ve considered nitpicky. I even value them more. 

But I also think there’s a difference between being capable of succeeding somewhere and being somewhere you can succeed as yourself. I spent nearly a year trying to overcome what I now recognize as incompatibilities, convinced that if I just worked harder or became more adaptable, I’d eventually feel like I belonged. 

And maybe that’s the lesson I’d offer anyone facing a PIP: Take the feedback seriously. Make the changes you need to make. But don’t confuse proving you can do a job with proving it’s the right job for you. And don’t be afraid to admit when something isn’t working and proactively change course. 

I have three-quarters of the bottle of Boss Fix Oil left. Just in case.

Matt Taylor has been elected mayor of the District of Okanagan Falls. According to Civic Info BC, Taylor received 780 votes to Tyler Johnsen’s 312 and Glen Innes’ 106. The Penticton Western spoke with Taylor shortly after he received the news himself. “I feel good,” said Taylor. “I think it was a decisive result, and I look forward to being able to benefit the community with having some experience in government.” Joining Taylor at the inaugural council table will be Amy Bydal, Allison Symons, Randy Ludwar and Eugene Dettling. A total of 1,207 ballots were cast in the election according to the preliminary results, out of a total eligible electorate of 2,360, which equates to about a 51 per cent turnout rate. “I would like to say thanks to the residents of Okanagan Falls for taking the time to show out in strong numbers for the vote,” said Taylor. ” I would like to say thanks for all the candidates, both at the mayor level and the councilor level, and the teams that worked with them, and obviously I’d like to thank my own supporters and my family for giving me the time.” Okanagan Falls’ residents voted in a 2025 referendum to incorporate as a municipality, the first to be established since 2016. The inaugural meeting of the District of Okanagan Falls’ new council will finish off the incorporation process on Nov. 6.

title: What actually motivates AI talent to work for companies
description:
Mark Zuckerberg hand-delivered homemade soup to OpenAI researchers’ front doors in an attempt to recruit them. Elon Musk pledged to personally read every SpaceX AI application—no résumé required; pedigree optional. When the world’s richest founders are cold-calling engineers with soup and big-figure job offers, it’s clear the AI talent war has reached a new, absurd level.

But Meta and SpaceX aren’t the only ones taking outlandish measures to attract talent in the tightest hiring market in tech history. The median base salary for startup engineers is $200,000, a 25% increase since 2022 and a far cry from the equity-first model that startups have relied on for decades. 

Artificial intelligence roles are taking a long time to fill, and there are plenty of them. AI, machine learning, and data science postings jumped 163% in 2025 from 2024, yet 72% of employers say they’re struggling to fill roles. The challenge isn’t just supply. It’s also a hiring strategy issue. The old model of a charismatic founder with a vision—and often no product yet—is out. AI talent wants to see hard proof, not a pitch deck. 

What AI talent responds to

I recently published research on how founders and AI specialists interact on CoffeeSpace, a platform focused on helping startups build early teams from cofounder matching to recruitment. The matching works like a dating app; users send invitations the same way you swipe on Tinder or Hinge. Except instead of singles searching for a match, founders and engineers decide whether to accept or decline an invitation to start a conversation. Of its roughly 25,000 users and 1 million swipes, we narrowed the analysis to 6,868 people involved in AI-relevant matches—357 of whom qualified as AI talent— across about 160,000 decisions.  

I found a disconnect between what founders think AI talent wants, and what AI talent is actually looking for.

Founder ambition and equity offers aren’t enough to pique a candidate’s interest anymore. Instead, AI specialists want to see momentum. Founders working full-time on their project were 20% more likely to have their invitations accepted than those still in the exploration phase. But momentum doesn’t require a finished product. A prototype and a handful of early users can signal that an idea has traction, which AI specialists want to see.

A PhD, an MBA, or a stint at Meta or Google used to matter. Today, they are weaker predictors than most founders assume. AI professionals are seeking out founders with nontechnical backgrounds. Founders with legal experience saw 18% higher acceptance rates; those with sales experience saw a 10% lift. 

The reasoning tracks. A founder with a legal background can lower perceived risks around compliance, IP, and contracts. A sales background demonstrates that a founder knows how to get products in front of paying customers, not just investors. Any professional experience outside of tech can signal to talent that this founder will let them focus on building, rather than reviewing investor decks.

Of course, AI specialists also make decisions based on compensation, equity, and remote work options, but later in the process than founders might realize. Perks like these don’t create interest on their own, but they can remove friction for candidates who are already in the negotiation stage.

What founders can do about it

Most founders can’t compete with Zuckerberg’s theatrics or Musk’s budget. The good news is that the data suggests they don’t need to.

People looking for top AI talent can make progress visible. Publishing a build log, sharing a demo video, or putting a working prototype in front of even a handful of users before recruiting begins can demonstrate momentum.

If a team is heavy on technical expertise, it may help to hire people with legal or sales experience before stacking the team with another engineer. Having a coworker with experience in these fields can do more to attract AI talent. And save the perks conversation for later, as flexible compensation and remote work options close deals rather than opening them.

AI pros want a viable prototype more than a soup delivery. They’d rather be left to work on the product than get sucked into strategy meetings. They want committed founders, not a Steve Jobs-like visionary running on charisma alone. In short, they want proof that what they’re building is real, and that the people building it are grounded. No amount of soup can make up for that.

National Defence Minister David McGuinty confirms there have been both fatalities and injuries after an incident at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. McGuinty provided the update in a late-night news conference in Ottawa Saturday. “I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base. McGuinty couldn’t provide specific numbers on those dead or injured. He called it an “active and delicate situation.” Wainwright RCMP responded to a request for assistance at CFB Wainwright on Saturday around 4 p.m., with early reports that there was a fire at a training area. McGuinty said his understanding is the fire is “still being monitored very closely.” He said they’re currently “working through the details of what actually occurred,” adding there will be “more to say in the coming hours and days.” McGuinty added the Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence, partners across the federal government including Public Safety, are working with the Government of Alberta and municipal governments. title: My phone is a noisy place
description:
A while back, I shared a note about how I had cut down my phone usage a lot and what it had changed for me.

And for a few months, I actually stuck to it.
But lately, I've been watching or listening to videos from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. And for the times when I can't watch videos (like when I'm walking in the street, for example), I will put a podcast or music to occupy the space.

I'm not sure why I went back to this sluggish state when I had been doing so well for a long time, but I think it's because I actually missed watching specific YouTubers and listening to specific podcasts. So I allowed some back into my life and then some more and eventually, it took over.

Which leaves me in a weird situation, because I now know that no YouTube at all is disappointing. There is some content that I actually like and don't want to stop watching, especially since it's only like at most 2 hours per week plus the occasional GeoWizard adventure.
But at the same time, I know that if I let these back in, I won't be able to stop myself, because there is a ton of content that I like, content that I wouldn't miss if I didn't watch it, but that is still nice to watch.
I could try an extension to hide the recommendations, but knowing me, I will probably deactivate it pretty quickly and find an "acceptable" reason why. Worth a try though, I guess.

The other thing that crept back is Spotify. I listen to music (or podcasts, but mostly music) when I'm not watching videos. On the one hand, it's great because I have discovered many new artists lately, but at the same time, I've been feeling more disconnected, irritated when someone is trying to talk to me and I have to remove my AirPods and, overall like my mind can never breathe.
I'd say that the thing that has changed since the last article is that now silence isn't weird anymore. I even enjoy it! But for some reason I always feel this need to listen to something. Plus, I have been questioning my relationship with music lately, but I will talk about it in another note.

Now again, I'm not sure about what the right thing to do is. I definitely don't want to stop listening to music, I enjoy it way too much. But I don't want it to be constant.
Trying to apply time restrictions won't work because I know that I will find "good reasons" to circumvent them.
Maybe something like "you can only listen to music when you do this and that" could work. This has worked for podcasts already, as there are some podcasts that I only listen to when cleaning and others I only listen to when grocery shopping.
Another idea would be to say "You can only listen to music out loud" and not in your AirPods. So that would automatically limit my time, because there are many situations where you can't listen to music out loud.

So where does this leave me? What about the things I said in the previous note about enjoying life without all this?
I guess it's as with all things in life, I need to find balance.

The approach to ditch all music and YouTube was certainly too extreme, but spending my whole days listening to stuff is also too extreme.
Another thing to consider is the fact that I tend to get absorbed by things, both the good and the bad ones.
So when I get to reading a book or programming something, I will just do it for hours upon hours to the point of forgetting to eat. But the same can be said for playing video games and watching videos, which has a much more negative impact.
And I don't know that I should change this, it's just a part of my personality, but I need to learn to put systems in place to prevent it for things that make me rot away.

I don't have a good conclusion yet. Honestly, I think that what would help me would be to have the opinions from a bunch of different people and see how they deal with all this, to try as many options as possible until I find the balance I'm looking for.

For now, I will try to limit Spotify and I will try YouTube "blocking" extensions. If you have any other ideas or want to share your experience, please email me, I'd be grateful to receive it.

I hope you have a great day, bye.

title: Apple Hires Former Meta Lawyer to Oversee Global Litigation
description:
Apple has hired former Meta lawyer Scott Tucker to lead its litigation team, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Tucker will become Apple's vice president of global litigation and financial services, a new position overseeing commercial lawsuits, patent disputes, and legal matters involving its financial products. He previously led litigation at ‌Meta‌ and held a senior legal role at Morgan Stanley.

The move brings Tucker back together with Jennifer Newstead, Apple's general counsel. Newstead joined Apple's leadership in March after six years as ‌Meta‌'s top lawyer.

Heather Grenier, who currently oversees Apple's commercial and competition litigation, will report to Tucker instead of Newstead. She will remain on Newstead's leadership team. Apple is also expanding legal executive Kyle Andeer's responsibilities to include international legal matters, child safety, cybersecurity, and law enforcement.

The changes are part of a wider overhaul under Newstead, who now oversees both legal and government affairs. Apple announced plans to combine the teams alongside the retirements of Kate Adams and Lisa Jackson.

According to Gurman, some Apple executives believe the company should have performed better in court, particularly in App Store disputes. Its battle with Epic Games has forced changes to the rules for links to outside payment options and the fees Apple can charge.

Apple also faces the U.S. government's antitrust lawsuit and privacy cases. Separately, it agreed to a $250 million settlement over delayed Siri features, with a final approval hearing scheduled for February 2027.

title: Dumas Sea Face Masterplan / INI Design Studio
description: For decades, Surat's relationship with the Arabian Sea was shaped by a fragmented and underutilized shoreline. The Dumas Sea Face Masterplan reimagines this edge as a living coastal landscape, transforming a neglected waterfront into a resilient public realm where ecology, civic life, and urban identity converge. Located along the historic Dumas coastline, the project responds to the growing demand for high-quality public open space in one of India's fastest-growing cities. Despite its long-standing cultural and recreational significance, fragmented development, limited accessibility, and the absence of a cohesive vision have constrained the shoreline's potential. The masterplan addresses these challenges by stitching together disparate segments into a continuous waterfront experience that reconnects the city with the sea.

title: Be honest about what your evals prove
description:
Your coding agent just scored 100% on an eval, and every criterion passed. There's only one problem: the code it generated doesn't build. How is that possible? The eval checked 20 aspects of the implementation. The agent used the right APIs and followed the expected patterns. It created the required files and included the necessary configuration. Every one of those checks passed, but nobody tried building the application.

The eval did exactly what it was designed to do. It verified the criteria it was given, and the agent met all of them. The problem starts with what we infer from that result. A 100% eval score means that 100% of the evaluated criteria passed. It doesn't tell you whether the agent completed the user's task.

The temptation of proxies

Ideally, an eval verifies whether the agent achieved the user's goal. If the user asks for a working application, you verify that the application works. In practice, that's easier said than done. Consider evaluating an agent that builds and deploys a cloud application. To verify that it succeeded, you'd need to build the generated code and provision the infrastructure. Then you'd deploy the application and exercise its functionality before cleaning everything up. Along the way, you'd have to handle failures and unpredictable outputs, sometimes for applications whose implementation you can't anticipate. A harness like that can take considerable time and money to build.

So we compromise. Instead of verifying that the application works, we check whether the generated code looks plausible. We inspect the files and configuration that the agent produced and compare its API usage against the patterns we expect. These checks become proxies for functional success, and there's nothing inherently wrong with that. Engineering is full of tradeoffs, and evaluating agents is no exception. Sometimes direct verification is impractical, and a proxy is the best evidence you can reasonably get. The trap is forgetting that we're measuring a proxy and communicating the result as proof of success.

Validation isn't the same as success

Agent skills show the same pattern. You can automatically verify that a skill's frontmatter is valid and that its structure follows the specification. You can even check whether the agent invokes the skill or whether its output contains certain strings. These checks are useful because they catch structural problems and regressions, much like linting or static analysis does in traditional software development. But none of them prove that the skill helps the agent complete the user's task.

Nobody claims that an application works because it passes linting. We treat static analysis and builds as different evidence from functional tests, and we validate performance and deployments separately again, because each of them tells us something different about the software. Agent evaluations deserve the same discipline. A skill that passes structural validation meets certain technical requirements. An agent invoking the skill is evidence that the skill was invoked. That's it. Neither, on its own, proves that the user got what they asked for, and even a comprehensive collection of proxy checks might miss the one thing that matters most.

What does your eval actually prove?

Before you publish an eval result, complete this sentence, and be precise about it:

When this eval passes, we know that…

If your eval checks implementation patterns without building the code, an honest answer sounds like this:

When this eval passes, we know that the agent generated code that satisfies our implementation criteria. We haven't verified that it builds or runs.

That's a defensible claim. What you shouldn't say is that the agent built a working application, because your eval never checked that. The same goes for the cloud application from earlier. An agent can generate infrastructure definitions and deployment scripts that look entirely correct, but until you deploy and validate the application, you don't know whether it works in the target environment. If a working deployment was what the user asked for, that's a significant gap in your evidence. An eval doesn't have to verify everything. You might deliberately accept that gap because direct verification costs too much, and that's your tradeoff to make. But the confidence you communicate should never exceed the evidence you've collected.

Don't let the nuance disappear

Imagine a team that reports consistently high eval scores. The results look excellent. Management sees progress that justifies the investment, and everyone believes that the agent experience is improving. Meanwhile, users complain that the generated applications don't work. How can both be true? Perhaps the eval scenarios don't represent what users actually encounter, or the criteria verify implementation details while missing functional failures. Perhaps both. Either way, the team has been optimizing against its eval results while gradually losing touch with what its users experience.

That's why a misleading eval can be worse than no eval at all. Without evidence, you know that you're uncertain. With a reassuring score that nobody fully understands, you might stop asking whether things actually work. So when users report failures despite high eval scores, treat that as a reason to revisit both your scenarios and your criteria. Your eval might cover different situations from the ones your users face, or measure outcomes other than the ones they care about.

Preventing this is primarily the job of the people who design the evals. They know what they measured and which compromises they made, so they also know what remains unverified. You can't expect everyone who reads the results to inspect the eval harness and reconstruct those limitations themselves. You can report them in a matrix of separate scores or in a short explanation. Either works, as long as the scope and limitations of the evidence travel with the results.

Be deliberate about what you measure

Proxies are often a practical response to how complex it is to evaluate real-world agent behavior. They're still compromises, though, and you should make them deliberately. Whenever possible, evaluate whether the user actually succeeded. When that's impractical, use the best evidence you can get and be clear about its limitations. Don't confuse validation checks with outcome evaluations, and don't let a perfect score imply more than you've verified. Before you celebrate your next 100% eval score, ask yourself: when this eval passes, what do we actually know? Then make sure that's also what everyone reading the results understands.

Less than a kilometre away lies the Dnipro, the river that has formed the frontline since Ukrainian forces liberated Kherson in November 2022; Moscow’s troops are on the opposite bank.

title: As King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know that Winston Churchill admitted to imperial plunder 90 years ago | Kenneth Mohammed
description:
Modern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on imperial plunder

For us in the Caribbean, there is something surreal about Britain’s renewed nostalgia over empire. As Britain’s monarch prepares to visit the Caribbean, and at a time when we in the former colonies are demanding to have a serious reckoning with slavery and reparations, UK politicians are invoking a dumbed-down distortion of history.

Rewriting the facts: the Reform MP Robert Jenrick has argued that colonies owed Britain a “debt of gratitude” for the institutions empire bequeathed them. Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former minister in a Conservative government, has described British colonialism as “one of the greatest civilising, prosperity-creating forces the world has ever seen”. The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, has disputed colonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations, former colonies should repay Britain for the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts.

title: Apple’s HomeView has a Google problem
description:
As someone who’s kept a smart display on the kitchen counter for the last eight years, I should be among the target audience for Apple HomeView.

My Lenovo Smart Display is one of the best gadgets I’ve ever owned, mainly because it’s always cycling through family photos that I’d otherwise surely forget. In addition to being a constant source of fond memories for me and my family, it is also occasionally useful for kitchen timers, music, weather forecasts, and managing the grocery list.

HomeView, which launches next month for $299, brings an Apple-like layer of polish to the smart display concept, with a high-resolution display, aluminum base, and built-in subwoofer. Its facial recognition capabilities also allow it to display each person’s messages and calendar events.

But for all those bells and whistles, HomeView appears to fall short on the one feature I care about most: Its photo features are designed around iCloud Photos, making it a tough sell for me and the other 1.5 billion people who use Google Photos. Without a steady supply of fresh photos, HomeView might wind up feeling a bit empty.

How HomeView works

Those who’ve seen the HomeView up close liken it to a giant Apple Watch, with a 7-inch square-shaped screen that provides information at a glance. The main “Faces” view cycles through things like the time, weather, and photos, and you can swipe up to a home screen for built-in apps and smart home controls.

At least at the outset, the emphasis is clearly on Apple apps and services such as FaceTime, Apple Music, Podcasts, and Safari. The role for third-party apps is more limited. If a music or video app is compatible with CarPlay, Apple’s in-vehicle projection system, Apple may provide similar access on HomeView when a compatible iPhone is nearby. This would allow users to access third-party music like Spotify. HomeView will also support third-party home screen widgets, similar to those on iOS.

As for photos, Apple hasn’t gone into much detail, other than saying it will offer “Portrait-style depth effects” and support for shared albums that “loved ones near and far can help fill.” Smart displays from Google and Amazon are both able to surface photos of specific people, including new photos that users upload to cloud storage over time, so hopefully that will be a possibility with HomeView as well.

Either way, Apple has not announced any provisions for displaying photos from outside its own ecosystem. Its photo frame features will likely rely on users’ iCloud Photos libraries exclusively.

Photos are the killer app

Although some folks have wondered about the HomeView’s target audience, I’ve always felt that photo frames are the ideal use case for a smart display. It’s a frictionless way to revisit all the smartphone photos you’ve taken, and it fits perfectly with the concept of a communal device for everyone in the home. Compared to stand-alone digital photo frames, I also like that these devices can do a little bit more, such as controlling smart home devices, playing music, and setting timers.

Without the photo component, though, a device like HomeView just becomes another screen in a home already filled with them. Using it as a photo frame is what justifies everything else. For me, at least, HomeView won’t be of much use if I can’t bring my Google Photos library with me.

While Google does offer an easy way to transfer your entire Google Photos library to iCloud Photos, I’d rather not switch photo systems just for the sake of a new gadget. Besides, I prefer Google Photos anyway as someone who doesn’t exclusively use Apple products.

To be fair, other smart displays are similarly closed-off to third-party photo sources. Google’s Nest Hub is for Google Photos, and Amazon’s Echo Show devices are for Amazon Photos. It’s not surprising that Apple would go the same route, because supporting other sources would create complications, and the whole point of HomeView is to reinforce Apple’s own ecosystem of services.

Still, my hope is that over time, Apple will expand the HomeView’s “Faces” feature to third-party apps. That way, alternative providers like Google Photos, Facebook, OneDrive, Ente Photos, and even the self-hosted Immich could provide a showcase for users’ photo libraries. Without a platform for external photos, the target audience for HomeView becomes a lot narrower.

title: On techno-solutionism
description:
I've been seeing more techno-solutionist talk online lately. Maybe it's just my algorithms that decided to show me more of that or maybe people are actually talking more about it. Either way, it made me think about this subject and it's implications, and also made me quite scared.

When I talk about techno-solutionism in this post, I mean it in relation towards climate change. Here's a definition to make sure we're all thinking about the same thing when reading this article.

Techno-solutionism is the idea that we will fix the climate crisis by using technology so we don't have to change our way of life.

Now let me preface by saying that I personally don't believe in techno-solutionism and I will develop why in this post. But even if you believe in it, I think you should read-on as my goal is not to judge or critisize but rather to ask questions and I think your answers would be as interesting as anyone else's.

The solutions that are often brought up in techno-solutionist discussions are Carbon Capture, AGI that will find the solutions for us, Geoengineering and Nuclear fusion.
As of now, none of these solutions are a reality. We are seeing progress in each of them, but they still pose many challenges that we are yet so solve.

The question then is, do we want to bet on things that we don't know for sure will ever become a reality? Because, you might strongly believe these will someday exist but you can't prove that they will. It's just a belief.
Personally, I don't want to throw the life of future generations of living beings to a bet.

Now, let's say this works and we actually figure these things out! What tells us that we'll figure them out in time?

Because while we are working on these solutions, the climate crisis is still going on. Living beings are quickly dying and becoming extinct, and even if you don't care about non-human forms of life, humans are dying too.

Are we as a species really willing to let so many other forms of life die for us to keep up with our current way of life?

Are we, the people living in privileged countries willing to keep exploiting other humans for our own profit and well being?

And can we really feel well and happy about how we'll live in a world where we have "fixed" the climate crisis but can still feel all the damages it caused?

Maybe your answer to all of these is yes, and maybe you'd even tell me that it's also possible that we will figure techno-solutions in time.
So let's say you are right about this, let's say that by 2050, we've found solutions that allow us to go to negative carbon emissions!

Then the question is, are you willing to let companies decide of the quality of the air you breathe?
Because since we live in a capitalist society, the companies running carbon capture machines and doing the geoengineering required to keep our current living standards will want to make profit.

They won't do it for the sake of being nice to us, when is the last time you've seen a company just be nice and gain profit off of it?

Now you could argue that we are already trusting companies for many really important things like electricity or transport of goods. But these aren't vital things.
People used to live without electricity and they would grow their own food, but no one would be able to live without breathable air.

My personal opinion on this is that I am definitely not ok with putting my survival and the survival of future generations in the hands of any company. And don't get me wrong, I would love to keep up the life that I currently have, it's so comfortable. And I so wish that every human going forward would have the same comfort of life that I have. But I simply don't think it is possible.

Maybe you are ok with the idea that only a few living beings will have a great life at the cost of all others, in which case, business as usual is perfectly fine. But I am not.

I believe that it is more than overdue that we start rethinking our future.
I don't want of a future where machines are what is keeping us alive like we are some sort of ill person surviving only because of their ventilator.

Let's use what we know and are sure of to build a new collective imagination. A world where yes, we will have lost a lot of our current comfort at the benefit of more equality, more mutual aid, more connexion to nature and each other, more time to think and dream.
A world where we can wake up every day without being stressed by an imminent wall that we seem to being sprinting towards at great speeds.

Sure, we won't be able to eat McDonalds, order stuff from the other side of the world for only a couple bucks and get it delivered the same day, drive a car to go buy food at the big nearby mall, travel for a few hundred euros/dollars to go virtually anywhere in at most 2 days, change phone as we please, etc

But isn't that worth it for the certainty that we and other livings, will be able to live for millennia to come?

We should stop being trapped in our current vision of the world and I'm hopeful that someday we'll look back on this time period like we are looking back on how they lived in the middle ages.

I would love to hear about you opinion on this subject, even if you disagree. So please feel free to send me a mail so we can discuss this matter further.

Have a nice day :))

excerpt: Conservative candidate for Juan de Fuca-Malahat Mike Hicks was under fire Friday for saying at an Oct. 9 debate that First Nations must be “conquered.” Hicks said in an interview that he meant that, by law, if a First Nation is unconquered, treaties must be negotiated. “In law, as I understand it, English law, you can’t just move into an area and take it over; you either have to conquer the First Nations in a war or sign a treaty,” he said. “And we did neither. And I’m all for it, of course.” Because a moderator cut him off after he said “First Nations have to be conquered,” it appeared as though he advocated for conquest. “That’s been misconstrued because people have just taken the part that was cut off,” he said. “I guess that’s the game I’m in,” he said. “It’s very disheartening.” Dana Lajeunesse, the NDP candidate for the riding, released a statement condemning Hicks’s choice of words. “Mike Hicks’s attempts to explain away his comments miss the point,” Lajeunesse said. “The word ‘conquered’ carries a long and painful history, and regardless of the point he was trying to make, there is no place for that kind of language today.” Green Party Leader Emily Lowan called on the Conservatives to remove Hicks from the party slate. “This isn’t one bad moment. title: New App Store Rules Target AI Deepfakes and Nudify Apps
description:
Apple today expanded its App Store moderation rules to cover AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery. Sexually explicit content was already banned, but now Apple says app developers must proactively prevent and remove AI-generated deepfakes from their platforms. Apple warns that apps with offending content could be removed from the ‌App Store‌ if developers fail to act.


The updated 1.2 rule names AI content creation apps and could be targeting apps like Grok, among others. Users have complained about xAI's Grok chatbot being used for nude and sexualized deepfakes, and earlier this year, Apple told xAI it would remove Grok from the ‌App Store‌ if it continued to permit nude deepfakes. xAI put safeguards in place, and Apple approved an updated version of the app.

Apple also added guideline 2.5.19 to clarify that developers who add features or functionality not present in the version of an app submitted for review risk removal from the ‌App Store‌ and Apple Developer Program. Apple links the rule to "nudification" apps that create sexually explicit images of real individuals without their consent, suggesting some of the apps have concealed their true purpose during review and added the nudify feature after approval.
Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as "nudification" — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch.

Along with changes focused on AI-generated content, Apple updated section 5 to extend its ban on apps that facilitate human trafficking or child exploitation to alternative app distribution.

"We do not hesitate to remove apps, and terminate the developers behind them, when they violate these guidelines," reads Apple's developer news post on the rule changes.

Apple's full updated guidelines can be found on its website.

BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says the money saved by building a bridge to replace the aging George Massey Tunnel would pay for construction of a new hospital for women and children south of the Fraser. At a press conference in Port Moody Friday morning (Oct. 16), Doerkson expanded on the previous day’s press release wherein the party committed to scrapping the planned eight-lane replacement tunnel in favour of a 10-lane “George Massey Bridge,” completing the Surrey Hospital in Cloverdale (which is already underway and set to open in early 2030), and building a new women and children’s hospital in Surrey. Thursday’s press release claimed a bridge would cut current commute times by up to 30 minutes and help businesses move goods more efficiently, but did not provide any specifics for how much the new bridge would cost, or when it might be complete. In August of 2021, the BC NDP government announced the Fraser River Tunnel Project, a new toll-free eight-lane immersed-tube tunnel featuring one dedicated transit lane in each direction and a separate multi-use path to support walking, biking and other active transportation options. The crossing, to be located immediately upstream of the 65-year-old George Massey Tunnel, came with a $4.15-billion price tag (updated in July 2026 to $8.5 billion) and an estimated completion date in late 2030 (changed this year to September 2031). Doerkson said Friday building a new bridge would cost $6 billion and take five years to build, adding it would be “more affordable” and could be “completed more quickly.” The $2.5 billion saved over the cost of a new tunnel would be used to fund construction of the new women and children’s hospital. title: El Niño winter forecast: See a map that shows which U.S. regions will get the most snow and rain
description:
This year’s Super El Niño “looms large” over the winter forecast for the United States, forecasters from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) wrote this week.

And for about half of the country, that’s shaping up to make for a wet winter. 

El Niño is a climate phenomenon defined by above-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, and a weakening of trade winds that flow from east to west. All those changes affect atmospheric conditions, disrupting global weather patterns.

How will the phenomenon impact U.S. weather patterns?

El Niños typically present with wetter conditions across the U.S. South, and drier than conditions farther north.

A 2026-2027 Winter Outlook map from NOAA illustrates that, showing a wavy band cutting across the U.S. that will bring “above normal” precipitation to the southern half of the country. That band swings up to cover the entire California coast and the East Coast, as well.  

Certain areas will be impacted even more: parts of Florida, for example, are forecasted to experience 70-80% above normal precipitation.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Niño will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS), said in a statement. 

That wet weather could ease drought conditions in the southwest. Southern Great Plains, Southeast, and parts of the East Coast, according to another NOAA map. 

But forecasters say that could make for other negative weather impacts.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides,” Graham said. “Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.” 

Some communities are already preparing. Governor Gavin Newsom of California has already declared a state of emergency ahead of this El Niño winter. 

With this El Niño already breaking records and potentially only getting stronger, “that can mean repeated rounds of heavy rain, strong winds, mountain snow, flooding, landslides, debris flows, large waves, and coastal flooding, especially when storms hit during very high tides” for California, according to his office. 

Certain areas of the country are expected to see drier-than-average conditions, though, like Hawaii, Alaska, the northern Mountain West, and some areas around the Great Lakes.

That also means drought conditions could “develop or worsen,” forecasters wrote, across some of the northern Rockies, as well as northeastern Oregon and eastern Washington.

Those forecasts mirror others looking ahead to this winter, including a series of maps from AccuWeather that was shared with Fast Company earlier this month.

Word to the wise: The map is not the territory

Experts do note that specific outcomes aren’t a guarantee; the El Niño simply tilts the odds toward certain impacts. As the season gets closer, meteorologists will continue to update their forecasts. 

For those who want to keep a close eye on any oncoming snow or rain, the NWS has now opened its Probabilistic Precipitation Portal, an interactive map that lets users see “the low-end, expected, and high-end amounts of snow, ice and rain” over a 72-hour period.

Somehow, as the models have gotten better, they've left something behind. I find myself thinking more and more wistfully of DALL·E 2, an image generation model from 2022 that conceptually shouldn't hold a candle to the current state of the art. So why do I miss it?

title: Developers Question Scope of Potential Apple Antitrust Settlement
description:
Developers are questioning whether a settlement of the U.S. government's antitrust case against Apple would meaningfully loosen the company's control over the iPhone, according to The Information.



The report highlights PayPal and Epic Games among the companies that have raised concerns with the Department of Justice (DOJ). Officials have reportedly indicated that they favor a negotiated resolution and have asked developers to suggest improvements to how the iPhone works with other companies' products.

These discussions largely center on interoperability, including access for competing accessories and payment services. The concern among developers and antitrust lawyers cited in the report is how much Apple would actually have to change. Rival smartwatches, for example, lack much of the integration available to the Apple Watch, while competing payment apps reportedly still face disadvantages despite gaining access to near-field communication (NFC) technology for contactless payments.

When the DOJ filed its lawsuit in March 2024, it alleged that restrictions affecting messaging, digital wallets, smartwatches, cloud gaming, and multipurpose apps helped Apple unlawfully protect its smartphone monopoly. Apple rejected these allegations and argued that the government's proposed intervention would threaten its ability to design integrated products.

Some of the capabilities at issue have changed since the lawsuit began. Apple added Rich Communication Services (RCS) support to Messages with iOS 18, improving communication with Android phones. It also expanded access to the iPhone's NFC capabilities for third-party contactless transactions starting with iOS 18.1.

According to The Information, Apple offered interoperability concessions during an earlier attempt to avert the lawsuit. The company could still resist the broader changes developers want, leaving the current negotiations without an agreement. Proton said it doubted Apple would accept terms developers would regard as satisfactory.

title: Journalist Wudan Yan on the importance of fact-checking as ‘peer review’
description:
Fact-checking in journalism can mean many different things — and the process can vary whether you're working on a book or podcast, a longform magazine feature, or a breaking story in a 24/7 newsroom. 

But given the rise of disinformation and AI content, we need fact-checking more than ever. And there's an opportunity to bring more clarity to the process, both for journalists and for our audiences.  

This week's guest on the Nieman Storyboard podcast, journalist Wudan Yan, is founder of the fact-checking agency Factual, which provides fact-checking services for journalists, authors, and nonprofits. Writing for her newsletter, she recently made the case that fact-checking itself needs to evolve to meet the moment, so we talked about how journalists can make the most of the process in their own work.


[ Follow us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. ]

“ My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care,” Yan told me. But “as long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.” 

Yan was pursuing a doctoral degree in cancer biology when she decided to make the jump into journalism, starting as a fact-checker for publications including the science magazine Nautilus. She eventually moved into reporting, developing an understanding for what it meant to tell science and environmental stories through a narrative lens. Her writing has appeared in The Atlantic, California Sunday Magazine, High Country News, MIT Technology Review, The New York Times, and Popular Mechanics, among other publications. 

The excerpts below are edited for length and clarity.

Defining fact-checking as a form of ‘peer review’

I think people value accuracy intellectually. … Humans who conduct fact-checking are expensive. We're not AI, and so there's a price to pay, and it's really important for me to work with clients who understand that value.

 I usually describe fact-checking as a peer review for accuracy in the same way that coming from my previous career as a scientist, you cannot peer review your own work in a journal for publication. Somebody else has to do that peer reviewing for you. So when you are writing for a daily newspaper, if you're just making sure that what you wrote that's about to go to press is accurate, you're double-checking yourself. You're not fact-checking yourself.

On organizing your reporting and taking time to process it

Early in my career, I got a really amazing glimpse into how other reporters organize their work, and that gave me frameworks for how to organize my own reporting. So I use Google Drive, and for a project like this turmeric feature [“The Vice of Spice: Confronting Lead-Tainted Turmeric"], that's the main folder. There are interview notes, audio files, research papers, and then another folder just called field reporting. Quickly, you're going to realize all I have in my life are these like Russian nesting dolls of Google Drive folders.

Then outside of Google Drive — I think this is an Ira Glass tactic — once you're done with all the interviews and field reporting from a day, you kind of just sit and basically journal about the day.

The way that I interpreted that advice was to write about my day as if what I discovered that day was going to be the lead of my story. So I did that every single day, even if there wasn't really a story and it was really boring. It just got me into a very cinematic way of writing.

Quite honestly, in many of the features that I have produced over my career, I am just plagiarizing off of myself when I start writing the lead. And I can't tell you how many hours it saves me there because I've already done that hard work.

On the future of fact-checking and journalism

 I think for fact-checking right now, I don't think the robots are going to come for this type of work yet. I went to a professional conference the other weekend, and just talking to people who are getting all these spammy emails from AI agents being like, "If you want us to verify a paper, send it to us, and it's $25, and we'll look at primary sources only and let you know how a claim stacks up." And nobody in my world is really taking that seriously. I'm curious about who's paying $25 for a robot to check a claim, or what's attributed to a single paper. AI can make a recommendation, but you still definitely need a human to make sure that whatever's coming up on Google search or Claude or ChatGPT actually makes sense for the context and the story that's involved. 

 My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care. … As long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.

title: This one factor will define the hospital of the future
description:
In 1960, British physician Lord Taylor published an essay in The British Medical Journal titled “Hospitals of the Future,” in in which he predicted that the hospital of the future would need to adapt its infrastructure to changing medical needs and organize care around patients.

Since then, discussions about the hospital of the future have tended to focus on a wide array of technologies, such as intelligent patient rooms, automated records, telemedicine, robots, and remote surgery.

Don’t get me wrong: these technologies matter. However, when it comes to the hospital of the future, Taylor’s fundamental observation remains critical: The hospital of the future will be defined by how well those solutions are coordinated around the patient.

A FRAGMENTED REALITY

Many hospitals today operate with infrastructure and technology that have been built over decades. The technologies that keep the hospital operational, from clinical records, staffing platforms, and financial systems to supply applications, were purchased at different times to solve different problems, creating fragmented systems.

In my career as an interventional cardiologist and now as a technologist, I have seen hospital leaders wrestle daily with questions that seem routine—even mundane—but are critical to patient care. For example: Which beds are available and adequately staffed? Which patients could be discharged? Which operating rooms are likely to run late? Are the supplies for tomorrow’s procedures in stock? Has a payer approved the next stage of care? Does this patient need the MRI performed during their inpatient stay, or can it be safely scheduled as an outpatient?

In this fragmented reality, the challenge is integrating new technologies with the existing systems in a way that fits into existing workflows and allows hospitals to function as a coordinated institution.  

The problem is rarely a lack of data. More often, the answer must be pieced together from multiple disconnected systems. The last decade has seen an explosion of data. Today, healthcare accounts for as much as one-third of the world’s total digital data, and hospitals have made considerable progress in digitizing and exchanging clinical information.

THE DATA VERSUS INSIGHTS IMBALANCE

This abundance of data is not currently translating into a corresponding surge of meaningful insights. Although 71% of hospitals said necessary clinical information was routinely available at the point of care, only 42% said clinicians routinely used it when treating patients, according to federal health IT data.

We’ve become adept at capturing data, but we have work to do translating it into actionable next steps.

Accomplishing this requires uniting multiple systems, including the electronic health record system, imaging queues, and laboratory systems, to name a few. Today, employees often must glean insights from disconnected sources, and even manual processes, to create an operating picture. For example, a nurse manager may believe a unit is adequately staffed for the day based on current census but may be unaware that additional patients are expected in the emergency department and that morning discharges are now occurring in the evening. A surgical scheduler may see an open operating room without knowing whether the required implant will arrive on time.

Coupled with rising patient volumes and more complex care cases, the status quo is untenable.

A HOLISTIC VIEW

Hospitals cannot replace decades of infrastructure overnight. But artificial intelligence can help close this gap—many hospitals are freeing up capacity to care for more people in their community, reducing costs, and delivering more timely care with this technology. The key is scaling its use.

AI is innately strong at spotting patterns in data, making it ideally suited to help hospital leaders derive meaningful, actionable insights from various data sources to address the complex challenges hospitals face in balancing patient demand, staffing, and hospital resources.

However, to fully realize Taylor’s vision, AI will need to help hospitals move from prediction to coordination. When an operating room schedule changes, staffing, supplies, patient preparation, and recovery capacity should adjust with it. When emergency demand rises, the hospital should be able to identify likely admissions, locate staffed beds, identify delayed discharges, and resolve routine obstacles before they become capacity problems.

The goal should be to create an operational layer that understands how a decision in one part of the institution affects another, all while keeping humans in control.

THE IMPORTANCE OF HUMAN OVERSIGHT

The goal is closed-loop execution: Identify a problem, act within the existing workflow, measure the impact, and provide the best alternative path when things change. Hospitals should never wonder whether an intervention reduced waiting, released capacity, or prevented delays.

AI should therefore be measured by more than model accuracy. There’s ideally just one indicator of success: Does this technology help elevate the quality of care efficiently?

That requires measuring how quickly recommendations become actions, how many manual handoffs remain, and whether outcomes improve. With human oversight, traceable data, and audit records, operational intelligence can reduce coordination work and help hospitals respond earlier.

Taylor concluded his 1960 report with this advice: “Put the patient in the center of the picture first, last, and all the time.”

Hospitals have spent decades building systems that record what happened. The hospital of the future will be defined by how well it coordinates what happens next.

Taha Kass-Hout, MD, is the global chief science and technology officer at GE HealthCare.

title: When AI Can Make Almost Anything, Judgment Becomes the Job
description:
Mike Taylor, Mike Taylor | Learning Designer, Speaker & Author, Oct 16, 2026

The argument here, stated about half way through the post, is that "when content becomes abundant, judgment becomes scarce." So "that is where learning professionals can bring more value." Let's think about that. A while ago I proposed a type of AI, called "deontic analytics", would decide what is worthwhile, what is valuable, what should be done. I've seen nothing that suggests AI will be incapable of this. Why would we trust human judgement over AI, if AI can be demonstrably better at this? Consider the new decision models, like Jev and Clef and Decision 1.0 (I'll be a human named that one). It's not obvious that human judgement will always be better. Image: Shadhin.

title: Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal
description: As one walks along the beachfront of Barcelona, the shoreline feels like it has always been there: sand, palm trees, a long promenade, restaurants, shops and modern hotels, when the reality is that it has not always been this way. Until the 1980s, Barcelona's seafront was a working barrier of railway lines, factories and informal housing, and wastewater ran straight into the Mediterranean. Starting in 1987, Barcelona has continuously created large promenades and passages between the city and the sea, creating an environment that today many might read as previously empty space, but is actually the result of decades of infrastructure and social complexity, along with a municipal effort to transform the city's territory and its relationship to the water. Following that transformation raises three questions that frame this article: who was displaced to open the waterfront, who governs it today, and who keeps it standing?

title: What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?
description: The buildings and construction sector accounts for around 39% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50 per cent of global material extraction. Operational carbon emissions which are associated with the energy consumed to run the buildings also rose by 1% to 9.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, even as building energy use intensity (EUI) has improved. These figures point to persistent gaps in the way buildings are designed, constructed and upgraded. One important area for closing those gaps is the building envelope insulation, which remains central to controlling energy demand, improving thermal resilience and reducing carbon emissions.

title: Lion Green Road by Mary Duggan Architects and RUFFARCHITECTS Wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
description: The RIBA Stirling Prize 2026 has been awarded to Lion Green Road, a housing development in Coulsdon, South London, designed by Mary Duggan Architects with RUFFARCHITECTS for Croydon Council. Comprising 157 homes across five residential blocks, the project combines privately owned and socially rented housing on a former car park. Presented annually by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), the Stirling Prize recognizes a building considered to make a significant contribution to the evolution of architecture and the built environment. The 2026 winner was announced at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate in London on October 15, marking the prize's 30th anniversary.

title: World Monuments Watch 2027 Nominations Point to Government Austerity, Climate Impact and Skills Shortages as Main Threats to Heritage
description: The World Monuments Fund (WMF), an independent nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of historic architecture and cultural heritage since 1965, receives nominations through the World Monuments Watch, a flagship advocacy and conservation program. Every two years, the Watch selects 25 sites from the nominations received from individuals and community-based organizations worldwide. Nominations for the 2027 World Monuments Watch closed on March 20, 2026, with a total of 372 public nominations from 84 countries and territories. Before announcing the selected sites in early 2027, the WMF offers an analysis of the nominations. Global data shows three main causes of heritage endangerment worldwide: government austerity, intensifying climate impact, and lack of access to specialized skills and expertise. At a time when political priorities tend to stray from history, the call is to recognize heritage sites as an area of shared opportunity rather than a burden.

title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
description:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

title: A protein that fuels cancer could also be the key to fighting it
description: Scientists have discovered how to turn a protein that normally fuels cancer growth into a weapon against it. By activating PPARD in immune cells, researchers made them better at burning fat and attacking tumors, slowing or stopping cancer growth in laboratory experiments. The approach showed promise against colorectal, breast, and ovarian cancers, as well as melanoma.

title: The Expanded Scope of the Architect: Moving Windmills Innovation Center
description: What do architects do? This age-old question reveals the perennial dichotomy between two aspects of building–how to construct, and why to build. Despite its ancient origins and its name deriving from Ancient Greek, the profession is one that has transformed over the centuries. Its present-day form, usually dated to the Italian Renaissance, makes a distinction between the act of building and the intellectual and aesthetic decision-making behind it. However, we may be in the midst of another nascent transformation. The commissioning of architecture has historically remained separate from the practice, but as can be seen in the work of MASS and projects like the Moving Windmills Innovation Center, this distinction is beginning to blur.

title: Carney urges Alberta voters to reject path to separation and nine other proposals
description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans at a Calgary rally Thursday to vote to keep the province in Canada and reject nine other referendum proposals in the Oct. 19 vote [timescolonist.com#1][cbc.ca#1]. The ballot does not decide independence directly: it asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or begin the legal process for a future binding separation referendum [oneindia.com#1][dw.com#1].

Carney warned that a vote against Canada could bring years of division and uncertainty, while acknowledging that Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa are real. He cited the proposed Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of federal support for the province. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who also supports remaining in Canada, argues that voters should approve the other nine questions to press Ottawa for more provincial autonomy [aa.com.tr#1][cbc.ca#1][calgaryherald.com#2].

A pro-unity rally is scheduled in Edmonton on Friday, and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to speak in Calgary. Voters cast more than 186,000 ballots in Wednesday’s advance poll, and Elections Alberta had received and processed 454,000 special ballots, according to figures reported by the Calgary Herald [timescolonist.com#1][calgaryherald.com#1].

title: Half of the world’s population has been exposed to heat waves and wildfire smoke at the same time
description:
Climate change is a global phenomenon, meaning that everyone, in some way, will feel its devastating impacts. 

And increasingly, those impacts are happening simultaneously: Over the past two decades, more than half of the world’s population has experienced simultaneous heat waves and wildfires, occurring on the same day, a study found.

Researchers at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, published their findings this week in the journal Science Advances.

The study looked at 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019. To see who experienced a wildfire, researchers looked at who was exposed to “fire-sourced air pollution”; their data took into account hourly temperature, fire emissions, air quality, and population information.

Over those 20 years, researchers found, the number of people around the world exposed to both wildfires and heat waves, on the same days, increased by 287 million—from 761 million people per year in the first half of that time period to more than 1 billion people per year in the second.

That means 55.9% of the global population has experienced at least one day where a heat wave and wildfire pollution occurred in tandem.

And the number of such days is increasing. From 2000 to 2009, the average person experienced one such day per year. Between 2010 and 2019, that rose to 1.7 days of co-exposure per person.

Damaging on multiple levels

The research doesn’t only illustrate how climate change is making extreme weather more frequent. It also shows how the health impacts of these events can compound as extreme weather overlaps.

Both heat waves and wildfires can cause serious harm to our health. Along with the risk of heatstroke—which can damage your brain, heart, and kidneys, and even be fatal—extreme heat and humidity can make it harder for some people to breathe, especially those with asthma or other lung conditions. 

Wildfires come with intense air pollution, full of tiny particles called PM2.5 (particulate matter 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter) that can get into our lungs and bloodstream, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and reduced lung function.

When heat waves combine with air pollution, the health impacts exacerbate. On days when an area sees a “double whammy” of high heat and high air pollution, the risk of death is three times greater “than the effect of either high heat or high air pollution alone,” health researchers have previously written. 

The Monash University researchers emphasize this in their study, too. “Compared with exposure to heat wave or landscape fire-sourced air pollution alone, co-exposure to both hazards may exert greater health impacts than the sum of their individual effects,” they write. 

In other words, the health risks—including respiratory and cardiovascular impacts—become amplified when wildfire air pollution and extreme heat happen together.

Extreme heat and wildfires also impact each event occurring. Conditions like high temperatures and dry soil promote wildfires, and wildfires then exacerbate heat waves because they release heat and pollution into the air.

“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heat waves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers wrote.

Which regions are being hit hardest?

Some regions of the world are experiencing these simultaneous effects more than others. Zambia, for example, sees more than 28 such days per person every year. The Democratic Republic of the Congo comes in second, with just over 24 days per person per year.

Countries with lower life expectancy, education, and income tended to see the highest amount of wildfire and heat co-exposure, an example of the way that climate change is hitting the world’s poorest countries the hardest. 

Still, almost every area of the world saw an increase in this trend.

Central America, South America, Central and Eastern Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of North America, Australia, and Russia all experienced “notable increases” in the annual average number of days that wildfire pollution and extreme heat occurred together.

title: A timeline of New York City trying to ban horse carriages in Central Park
description:
The iconic but controversial horse-drawn carriage industry in New York City might finally come to an end as Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin reached a deal Tuesday to outlaw them.

If enacted, the bill would ban rides for hire starting June 1, 2028. 

Other NYC mayors have contributed to this effort, but none facilitated a full ban. Mamdani could be the first to achieve the full support of the City Council to effectively ban horse-drawn carriages.  

How prior mayors dealt with carriage controversies

When a horse collapsed from exhaustion in 2011, then-Mayor Michael Bloomberg dismissed a call to ban the industry, citing the importance of maintaining a livelihood of New York City’s carriage drivers.

In 2013, former Mayor Bill de Blasio was the first mayor to announce plans for a full ban. Without support from the City Council, however, the effort proved fruitless.

Just months before the end of his mayorship, de Blasio’s successor, Eric Adams, attempted to end horse-drawn carriage operations, which also lost due to a lack of support from the City Council. 

Why is Mamdani acting now?

An 18-year-old tourist from India, Romanch Mahajan, died after falling from a runaway carriage in July, which prompted “Romanch’s Law.”

The legislation will phase out the carriages while also providing a plan for protection of the workers whose livelihoods rely on the popular tourist activity. This time around, council members are expected to support the ban, after Menin publicly endorsed the law in July.

“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani said in a statement on X on Tuesday. 

What’s at stake for the industry?

The industry salary is estimated at $65,000 to $70,000 per year, with approximately 68 active licenses and just under 160 horses licensed at the end of last year, according to the City Council’s Committee on Health.

As of May 3, 2025, the maximum fare for a carriage ride is $72.22 for the first 20 minutes, plus $28.89 for each additional 10 minutes. 

The 163-year-old industry brings tourism dollars into the city, although current estimates for just how much are hard to come by. (We’ve asked the NYC Horse & Carriage Alliance for more details.)

But it’s also yielded unsafe conditions for the horses and passengers. There have been 40 horse deaths between 1982 and 2026, the Manhattan borough president’s office found.

As the city moves toward a ban, the mayor is taking workers into consideration in the next stages.

CarriageOn, a coalition of carriage operators, cites itself as a diverse workforce, with immigrants at the forefront of its operation. There are questions about the future of these carriage operators, which the Mamdani administration aims to address.

The mayor’s office has been working on a detailed plan for the transition of the workforce and industry, a spokesperson on Mamdani’s team told Fast Company. 

Why does NYC have the horses in the first place?

Horse-drawn carriage rides for tourists date back to when Central Park opened in the 1800s, when carriages were already a mode of everyday transportation. Even then, people cited concerns about the horse-drawn vehicles. 

One of the most outspoken organizations is the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA), which was founded in New York City in 1866 amid a growing concern about the well-being of horses in the city.

Its original logo brandished an image of a carriage operator abusing a horse, while an angel hovered over the animal. Cruelty toward horses was a driving factor for the organization’s foundation, but horses also remained a vital part of transportation in the city. 

What would a ban mean for the horses?

As the tradition phases out, the horses need somewhere to go.

“If Romanch’s Law is enacted, the ASPCA stands ready to support the City through this transition,” ASPCA president and CEO Matt Bershadker told Fast Company. The organization is ready to provide “grant funding or other resources if necessary to help ensure humane placement and a safe future for every horse in need of a home,” he added.

Speaker Menin announced on Wednesday that the full council will vote on October 22 on the legislation.

“We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all,” Sneha Choudhary, deputy press secretary for the mayor’s office, told Fast Company.
