title: We can’t keep guessing whether AI helps students learn
description:
On September 2, as students returned to class, New York City implemented a one-year pause on generative AI use for nearly 600,000 students across pre-K, elementary, and middle school. Los Angeles soon followed, blocking it for every student on a district-issued device. Together, the country’s two largest school systems came to the same conclusion: Better to wait a year than to keep putting untested tools in front of kids.

Neither district is calling the decision permanent. Both are responding to parents who worry that untested AI tools are reaching students before anyone knows whether they improve learning. New York City Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said it best: “We’re standing firmly in our belief that innovation does not mean more technology, and over the next year, we will lead with evidence to make sure technology serves learning—not the other way around.” 

That leaves an obvious question: Where will that evidence come from?

ADOPTION IS OUTPACING EVIDENCE

Teachers, school leaders, parents, and students are making consequential decisions about AI without reliable information about what works, for whom, and under what conditions.

Sixty percent of teachers use AI for work, yet 82% report they’ve received no formal guidance on how to use it. Just half of middle and high schools have any AI policy, and only 6% of teachers in those schools say those policies are clear. This lack of clarity shows up in how people feel about AI, too. Thirty-one percent of Gen Z now say AI makes them angry, up from 22% a year earlier, and 80% believe relying on it will make learning harder.

Still, banning AI in school won’t take it out of students’ lives completely. A recent Common Sense Media survey found that 91% of teens ages 13 to 15 use AI for schoolwork or homework. And with 21% of adults already using AI at work, students need to consider the growing role of AI in their future careers.

It makes sense that school district leaders, educators, and families want to know when AI adds to student learning and when it takes away from it. But even with the best intentions, it’s hard to write good policy, train teachers, or make smart purchasing decisions when the evidence underneath is this thin.

WHAT WASHINGTON SHOULD DO

Congress and the federal administration have a chance to put the existing infrastructure to work and provide the evidence we need to safely and confidently advance student learning. The Alliance for Learning Innovation worked with AI researchers, practitioners, and our coalition of more than 150 members to develop federal recommendations on this exact topic. Four main takeaways:

  1. Pass the NEED Act. This past September, Senators Michael Bennet (D-CO), Thom Tillis (R-NC), and Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) reintroduced the bipartisan NEED Act, which would create a national center at the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) to develop and test bold new approaches to teaching and learning.

The model comes from the Pentagon’s Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), which helped build the early internet and laid the groundwork for Siri. Like DARPA, the new center would be run by expert program managers who can quickly move money to promising and high-impact ideas, invest more when they show results, and pivot when they don’t.

  1. Study AI tools with robust data. One example of how to study the issue: New York City plans to run AI pilots in a small number of high school classrooms this year to learn what’s working for its own students. The federal government should help school districts nationwide do the same.

Where pilots aren’t feasible, a coordinated national network of testbeds, combining real classrooms with synthetic environments that simulate how students use AI, would let researchers test tools across diverse schools and communities. The result would be practical evidence about how AI holds up in the everyday reality of teaching, plus clearer signals for developers and investors about which tools deserve to scale. Federal investment in these testbeds would give schools a shared, safe way to judge what is and isn’t working in classrooms.

  1. Measure what students learn. Many current evaluations can’t tell the difference between a student’s output and AI. Federally funded AI studies should measure how students perform with a tool, then evaluate them again on the same topics later without it. The American Psychological Association made the same case, urging that any AI-powered learning tool be judged by what students can do after they stop using it.

This is exactly the kind of rigor the Department of Education’s own guidance and a growing number of outcomes-based contracting models (which tie vendor payment to results), are asking for. Currently, few evaluations consistently meet this standard.

  1. Give school districts a common evaluation tool. Districts are evaluating AI tools without a clear definition of what makes it safe, effective, and ethical. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) already published a voluntary framework for AI Risk Management that organizations use across industries. IES should partner with NIST to build an education-specific version, aligned with the EDSAFE AI Alliance’s SAFE Benchmarks, that gives states and districts shared standards for judging tools on learning impact, safety, privacy, and transparency before those tools reach classrooms.

THE CLOCK IS TICKING

New York City was clear that this moratorium lasts one year for a reason. The city said it will spend that time studying how AI affects students, and Los Angeles and other districts have set similar deadlines.

That study shouldn’t happen one district at a time, and it shouldn’t be limited to the contexts of large and urban school districts. If we invest in our federal research infrastructure now, we can build a trustworthy evidence base across the country so that all students walking into class in Fall 2027 have access to tools that we know work.

Sara Schapiro is executive director of the Alliance for Learning Innovation.

title: Dementia cases are expected to more than double by 2050. A new study reveals who’s most at risk
description:
More and more of our loved ones could develop dementia, as the number of diagnoses is projected to more than double by 2050, according to new research.

In the absence of large-scale prevention efforts, the number of people who are diagnosed with dementia each year could total 24.7 million by 2050, up from 11.4 million in 2023, according to a study by Australian researchers published in JAMA Neurology. Women and people who live in low- and middle-income countries already have higher rates of dementia, a trend that’s likely to continue, according to the findings.

While the researchers didn’t pinpoint an exact reason why dementia affects populations differently, they say the prospect of more cases warrants urgency in investing in prevention efforts. The prospect of 24 million new cases of dementia each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems and economies around the world,” Henry Brodaty, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales Sydney and a co-author of the study, said in a statement.

“We cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” Brodaty said. “We need to act across the spectrum—from reducing modifiable risk factors and identifying people at risk earlier, through to improving diagnosis, treatment and care.”

The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people diagnosed with dementia spanning 18 countries or territories on six continents. They found that the incidence was somewhat higher among women—at 10.6 cases per 1,000 people versus 8.6 for men—but the difference was even starker depending on where people lived. The incidence of dementia was 13.6 cases per 1,000 people in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.

Understanding the populations who are most at-risk for developing dementia will be key to developing prevention, diagnosis and care strategies, according to the study’s authors. 

“The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population aging while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care,” Perminder Sachdev, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales in Sydney and a senior author of the study, said.

THE FINANCIAL TOLL OF DEMENTIA

Aging populations are understandably one of the main reasons why dementia cases are expected to increase, as this condition that affects memory, thinking and the ability to perform daily activities is more common after the age of 65. As of 2021, an estimated 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia, according to figures from the World Health Organization, and it’s the seventh leading cause of death.

The World Health Organization likewise estimated that as of 2019, dementia cost economies around the world about $1.3 trillion, so a surge in new cases also carries a financial toll. 

That’s why the new research should sound an alarm, as Dr. Liron Sinvani, director of research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging and a professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research in New York, told U.S. News & World Report. “It’s an accelerating epidemic that demands immediate attention.” 

And that’s especially important as the countries that will face an “enormous wave” of dementia cases also have very limited infrastructure to respond, as Sinvani told the outlet. 

“Health systems must prepare for this massive increase in diagnostic and care demand, and this is especially true for these low- and middle-income countries where the growth will be fastest,” she said. “We know that dementia care requires a lot of caregiver support and is very costly. We will need a better infrastructure.”

title: Government has perfected awarding grants
description:
The federal government sent $1.26 trillion to state and local governments in FY2022, primarily through grants. States distributed $662 billion to local governments, while nonprofits received $294 billion in government grants that year.

Grantmaking is essential to turning public policy into local action. Today, state agencies use grants to equip organizations to do everything from improving rural health and preventing homelessness to expanding broadband access and spurring economic development.

Most agencies already have a system for the transactional side of moving funds. There’s software for tracking the applications, awards, drawdowns, and procurement. The financial machinery of a grant is mature. But it wasn’t built to answer the question that matters most: Is the money working?

Beyond transactions and compliance, that’s a question about grantee needs and performance.

TODAY’S SYSTEMS SUPPORT THE GRANT

The answers to whether grants are working are scattered across spreadsheets, inaccessible shared drives, and a handful of annual reports.

But grantees are people, often working at community organizations, faith-based organizations, and other nonprofits, ranging from three employees to thousands. Today’s grant management systems don’t connect with those doing the work.

Does the executive director who inherits a grant midstream have what she needs? Can a frontline public servant get an answer in two days? When federal guidance shifts, is there any mechanism to broadcast the change to everyone who needs to know? Does the grantee have the organizational capacity to do this again, or is it being held together by one person who could leave?

We call the work of supporting grantees after an award “post-award delivery.” It exists to answer the question: Did it work?

GRANTEE SUPPORT IS AD HOC

A program officer’s actual job involves collecting the required documents, chasing outcome data on a cycle, and keeping some record of what was said to whom. The tools at their disposal weren’t built for the work. Contacts live in spreadsheets. Guidance goes out as an email attachment. And there’s no communication trail, just an inbox and whatever the last person remembers telling someone.

The cost isn’t evenly distributed. The best-resourced grantee asks the most questions, because someone there has “call the state” in their job description. The three-person nonprofit asks none because it doesn’t have the bandwidth to know what it doesn’t know, and it suspects admitting confusion won’t help next year’s application.

Tighter oversight doesn’t help here. Recipients need support. A grantee who can find an answer without waiting, who knows the agency is trying to make the job easier, is a grantee who trusts the process enough to ask for help before something breaks.

A COMPLEX CHAIN OF GRANTORS AND GRANTEES

State agencies are simultaneously grantees and grantors, often from the same desk in the same week. They receive federal funds with requirements attached, then distribute them to their partners with a layer of state requirements added.

Every fracture repeats at every tier. The state waiting on federal clarification has subrecipients waiting on it. Questions travel up the chain slowly and answers come back slower, and the organization at the bottom absorbs the accumulated latency of the entire structure.

BETTER METRICS TO UNDERSTAND GRANT EFFICACY

Today’s metrics measure the money’s movement. They’re process-oriented. We believe there are three metrics worth adding to understand grantee performance and improve program effectiveness.

  1. Agency throughput. How much time passes between appropriation and dollars doing work in the field, measured at the agency level across years rather than grant by grant?
  2. Capacity. Can this recipient run the program next cycle with less support than it needed this cycle?
  3. Cohort variance. The average grantee doesn’t exist. A cohort where 15 organizations are thriving and 20 are underwater reports the same average as one where everyone is merely muddling through. Aggregate numbers can’t tell you about the specific challenges.

With the right infrastructure, struggling grantee organizations can be clustered by size, region, or prior grant experience. Patterns emerge. Operations improve.

THE QUESTIONS ARE THE DATA

Recipients generate a continuous stream of intelligence that grantors currently discard.

Question volume and sophistication reveal a lot. If everyone is still asking foundational questions six months in, the program design has a problem. A cluster of questions from one region is an early warning. A recurring question is a documentation gap.

But today this data is functionally inaccessible. It’s scattered across inboxes, call notes, and untranscribed office hours. Structure it, and two things become possible:

  1. Routine questions get answered instantly against cited, approved guidance.
  2. Clustering surfaces emerging implementation problems while there’s still time to act.

The same infrastructure that lets grantors capture data also gives grantees a well-run program: a living repository of guidance, peers they can find, and one place to ask questions and see what others have already asked. Recipients who can see each other reduce the load on the agency.

It’s a shift from one-to-one to many-to-many. One answer, given once, available to every current and future recipient. Knowledge survives turnover, lasting beyond the period of performance.

BETTER GOVERNMENT FOR ALL

State agencies don’t want to be compliance enforcers. They want grantees to succeed and already invest enormous effort in helping them do so.

What’s missing is infrastructure that lets their guidance, expertise, and support reach every recipient when it matters. When agencies can identify challenges early, share answers once, and build capacity across a cohort, grantees perform better. Grants, in turn, deliver more for the communities they were designed to serve. Concretely, that means more veterans connected to housing and benefits, more communities connected to broadband, and more rural patients reached.

Getting post-award delivery right is the critical last mile between public funding and visible impact.

Madeleine Smith is cofounder and CEO of Civic Roundtable.

title: Meshtastic Offline GPS Tracking: Save Your Route Without a Phone
description:
A Meshtastic device can send its GPS position over the air, but that is not the same as keeping a track on the device itself. In the standard setup I was using, disconnecting the phone meant the node continued broadcasting its location without saving a local history for later. 

I wanted something simple: take a node out for a walk, leave the phone disconnected, and download the route when I got home. So I modified the Meshtastic firmware to add on-device GPS location caching. 

I have this running on a SenseCAP T1000E and a Heltec T096. Both remain Meshtastic nodes, with their normal communication functions, but now they can also record a route independently of the phone. 

 


Key Takeaways

The custom firmware records GPS points on the node without a connected phone.
A 500-point cache provides roughly eight hours of recording at one point per minute.
Reconnect to Meshtastic to load saved positions, then export them as GPX.
Clearing app history does not clear the tracker cache; use the device controls to remove saved points.

Table of ContentsWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware AddsUsing the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000ESyncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic AppExporting Your Route as a GPX FileClearing the Tracker CacheInstalling the Firmware and Exploring the CodeWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware Adds

Meshtastic is open source, and its module system gives you a useful way to add your own functionality without creating an entirely separate application. My modification adds a local cache for GPS points, controls for starting and stopping recording, and a way to replay those saved positions into the Meshtastic app. 

The basic workflow is: 


Start tracking on the device.
Go walking or travelling without a connected phone.
Reconnect to the Meshtastic app afterward.
Let the saved positions populate the map.
Export the track to GPX if you want to use it elsewhere.


The device still sends position updates over the air as normal. Local recording is an additional function, not a replacement for Meshtastic communication. You can still receive messages and hear the usual notification sounds while recording your route. 


500 points, recorded once per minute


In this build, I set the cache capacity to 500 location points. With automatic recording every minute, that gives you roughly eight hours of tracking capacity, provided the device has a GPS location to save. 

That figure describes the number of points the cache can hold, not a battery-life measurement. You can also build up a collection of points across separate outings. One of my test devices had 205 points collected during experiments over about a month, while the other contained routes from several days of walking. 

Using the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096

The T096 still has the familiar Meshtastic screens. I added one extra page for the tracker, showing whether recording is on or off and how many points are cached. 

For example, the display can show tracking switched off with 205 of 500 points cached. Stopping recording does not remove those points. They remain available to download later. 



To start recording: 


Navigate to the tracker screen.
Long-press the button to open its menu.
Select Start Tracking.
Check that the tracker screen changes to Tracking On.


With tracking enabled, the firmware saves a location every minute when a GPS position is available. The cached-point counter increases as points are recorded. A count of 205, for instance, becomes 206 after the next successful recording. 

To stop, open the menu again and select Stop Tracking. This stops the extra local recording function. The node continues doing its normal Meshtastic work, including sending positions according to its configuration. 

The same menu also includes Clear Cache, but save that until you have downloaded or exported anything you want to keep. 

Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000E

The T1000E does not have a screen, so I implemented the tracker controls through its button. The idea is to make it useful on its own, without needing to pull out a phone just to start a walk. 




Button action
Tracker function




One press
Save the current location to the cache.


Two presses
Start or stop automatic recording every minute.


Three presses
Clear the cached locations.




A double press starts recording with an audible beep. While recording, the device beeps every minute as it records. Double-press again to stop. 

The single-press action is handy when you just want to record where you are right now, rather than run continuous tracking. It writes that current location into the same cache. 

These shortcuts belong to this custom firmware. They are not instructions for the standard T1000E firmware. 

Syncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic App

Once you return, connect to the device through the Meshtastic app as usual. There is no separate tracker app required for this part. 


Scan for nearby devices in the app's connection screen.
Select the node you used for recording.
Open that node's details and its Position history.
Allow the connection to finish and the cached positions to arrive.


The position history may initially look empty. In my demonstration, the connection indicator was orange while connecting, then turned green. Once connected, the saved positions started arriving and the route filled in on the map. 


  
  The saved points populate the map after the node reconnects.


On my T096, the downloaded history included driving routes as well as the walking route I use regularly. Connecting to the T1000E brought in its own saved points from several days of walking. Apparently, I do quite a lot of walking! 


Deleting app history does not clear the device


This is an important distinction: the app's position history and the device's cache are separate. 

I deleted the position history in the app, disconnected, and connected again. The device replayed the saved positions, and the route appeared again. The points were still on the node. 

So, if a route returns after you delete it from the phone, that is expected. To remove the source of that replay, you need to clear the cache on the tracker itself. 

Exporting Your Route as a GPX File

Once the positions are in the Meshtastic app, you can export them as a GPX file and open the result in another mapping application. 

I exported a test track, gave it a name, then opened it through the file browser in GPX Viewer. The same route appeared there, this time drawn over its map. 



The process is straightforward: 


Wait for the cached positions to finish loading into Meshtastic.
Use the position-history export option to save a GPX file.
Give the file a name.
Open it in GPX Viewer or another application that supports GPX.


I also included a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat. It provides another way to export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app. The repository documentation explains that option. 

Clearing the Tracker Cache

After saving your route, you can clear the device's cached positions so they no longer replay into the app. 


T1000E: Press the button three times.
T096: Long-press to open the tracker menu, select Clear Cache, and confirm that you want to clear it.


On the T096, the counter returns to 0 of 500. After I cleared the cache and reconnected, the old saved route no longer arrived. A current location could still appear, but that was a fresh position rather than the previous cached history. 

If you want to remove the route from both places, clear the app's history as well as the device's cache. Export anything important first. 

Installing the Firmware and Exploring the Code

I put the firmware, source changes, and instructions in the tracker-firmware GitHub repository. It includes builds for the T096 and T1000E, device-control documentation, installation notes, and the Windows export tool. 

Before flashing, back up your Meshtastic configuration and export your keys. Do that first, before changing the firmware. 

For the demonstrated devices, installation uses the familiar flashing-mode and drag-and-drop process: 


Back up your existing configuration and keys.
Download the firmware file that matches your device.
Put the device into flashing mode.
Drag and drop the matching firmware file onto the device's flashing drive.


The flashing instructions shown for the T096 use two presses of Reset to make the drive appear. For the T1000E, hold the button while connecting the charging cable. Follow the repository's device-specific instructions rather than assuming that every Meshtastic board flashes the same way. 


How the modification fits into Meshtastic


I used Meshtastic 2.8.1 for the demonstrated build. The tracker changes can also be incorporated into another firmware version and compiled, rather than being tied only to that build. 

The source changes are concentrated in four files. Part of the work changes the button-handling thread, because the tracker needs those additional button actions. The rest uses Meshtastic's optional add-on modules, which provide a place for custom functionality to run inside the firmware. 

I also compiled an ESP32-S3 version, mentioning Heltec V3 and V4 hardware as additional targets. That is separate from the hands-on T096 and T1000E examples here, so check the available files and instructions for your particular board. 


The LoRaWAN edition is a separate project


I have a similar tracker project for the T1000E LoRaWAN edition, with comparable single-press and double-press controls. That project is aimed at LoRaWAN rather than Meshtastic. 

Do not confuse the LoRaWAN-edition firmware with the Meshtastic tracker build. There are supporting write-ups and architecture diagrams on the resource hub, but the firmware must match the device edition and the system you intend to use. 

What I like about this modification is how little it changes the everyday experience. It is still a Meshtastic node. It simply remembers where it has been, so you can take it out on its own and bring the route back afterward.

Frequently Asked Questions


Does offline tracking stop the device from working as a Meshtastic node?

No. The modification adds local location caching while retaining normal Meshtastic communication, including position broadcasts and message reception. 


Does the tracker save a point every minute without a GPS location?

The automatic recording interval is one minute, but the device needs a GPS position available to save a location point. 


Why do deleted tracks return when I reconnect?

Deleting position history in the app does not remove the points cached on the device. Reconnecting allows the node to replay them. Clear the device cache if you no longer want those saved positions to return. 


Can I export tracks without the Meshtastic phone app?

Yes. The repository includes a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat that can export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app.

title: Americans are warming to a healthcare idea that once seemed politically impossible
description:
Americans have hit a breaking point with health insurance.

Saddled with growing medical bills and totally reliant on stable jobs to stay healthy, the majority of Americans now say they would prefer a government plan that offers health insurance to everyone. 

Two-thirds of U.S. adults now support a national healthcare plan or “Medicare for All,” according to recent polling from health policy research group KFF. That’s a dramatic increase from 2020, when 53% of U.S. adults favored universal healthcare through a government plan, an option common among other wealthy nations. 

In the poll, 32% of respondents said they would “strongly favor” a single government healthcare plan that provides insurance for all Americans. An additional 34% of those polled said they would “somewhat favor” the overhaul to the U.S. healthcare system, with just 15% saying they “somewhat oppose” the idea and 19% saying they “strongly oppose” it. In the KFF poll, 84% of Democrats and 72% of independents were in favor of a national health insurance plan, compared with 34% of Republicans.

Another survey published this week by Axios-Ipsos confirmed the swell of support for reinventing the current U.S. healthcare system. In that poll, 43% of respondents said they would support a Medicare for All proposal that would replace the current private health insurance system. In that poll, 24% of respondents said they would oppose such a plan, while 32% reported being “unsure.” More Democrats (62%) and independents (47%) favored a government-run healthcare system, while a slight majority of Republicans opposed the idea (52%).

Crushing healthcare costs

Soaring support for a government-run health insurance system isn’t a mystery. Americans spend more on healthcare than people in other wealthy countries, but the U.S. government spends more, too—even without a broad national plan that insures everyone. Somehow all of that spending still adds up to worse health outcomes. In spite of spending twice what many of its peer countries spend per capita on healthcare, Americans live shorter, less healthy lives.

Americans are paying more and getting less when it comes to healthcare—and that spending is stretching them thin. In the richest country in the world by many measures, people are skipping doses of their meds and even buying less food to afford their rising healthcare costs. 

In the new Axios-Ipsos poll, 69% of Americans said they were worried about the rising cost of healthcare, with the same percentage reporting that a 10% increase in costs would hurt their family’s financial situation. A shocking 100 million Americans were already crushed under the weight of medical debt in 2022, and the situation is unlikely to improve given recent cuts to Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies. In 2024, Americans took out $74 billion in loans to pay their medical bills, with most borrowing more than $500.

U.S. voters fed up with the current state of health insurance will have a way to voice that displeasure soon. Progressive Democrats in some key November battleground races are running on a push for Medicare for All, but the party’s center and its leadership have yet to warm up to the idea in spite of soaring support among their constituents.

title: Healthcare has a churn problem
description:
I was diagnosed with anorexia at 10 years old. Over the next several years, my family and I navigated a healthcare system that was mostly focused on how many days I stayed in a hospital bed instead of whether I was getting better.

I spent my entire freshman year of high school in and out of facilities, counting down 45-minute therapy slots while fighting a brain disorder that forces you to battle your own mind upwards of six times a day. The bills came in, claims were processed, and the checkboxes were ticked, but I was still struggling with anorexia.

Decades later, now as a founder and CEO of an eating disorder treatment program, I realize my teenage experience embodied the traditional healthcare business model to a T.

THE ONLY INDUSTRY WHERE PRODUCT FAILURE IS PROFITABLE

In traditional healthcare, revenue is tied to volume: More time in session results in more revenue. The more appointments booked, the more the facility can bill; the longer someone stays in treatment—and the more times they relapse—the more profitable the facility becomes.

If any consumer tech or hardware startup ran on this model, it would fail fast. It’s like going to an auto repair shop that charges by the hour, sends you home with a car that still stalls, and then charges you again when you have to tow it back into the shop.

The main problem is industry alignment. Fee-for-service models reward visit volume and usually lead to fragmented, episodic care. Value-based outcome models, on the other hand, tie reimbursement directly to clinical and financial outcomes. If we want a healthcare system that can keep up with rising costs and demand, we need to align incentives around real, measurable outcomes.

BUILD WHAT WORKS

Tying financial compensation to real-world outcomes gives leaders the flexibility to build better products that result in positive outcomes for all parties involved. In healthcare, that means patients, their families, providers, and health insurance plans.

For example, when we started Equip, we knew that once-a-week therapy wasn’t enough to address a complex eating disorder, but the traditional fee-for-service billing system made it nearly impossible to bill for anything else. By partnering with forward-thinking health insurance plans to develop value-based payment structures, we designed the treatment model families needed: a team of doctors, dietitians, therapists, and coaches delivered virtually. This approach provides the right dose of care when patients need it, without uprooting their daily routines or stopping them from building a life worth living.

WHAT DOES “GOOD” LOOK LIKE?

The catch, however, is that the healthcare industry has historically lacked a consensus on what “good” means. Defining quality is particularly difficult in eating disorders, where recovery isn’t as simple as a blood test or a healed bone. The field uses two tools—the EDE-Q and the PARDI-AR—to set severity thresholds, but neither gets into what “getting better” means. It also requires a long-term view, which can clash with an industry where most health insurance plans operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles.

When I was 10, that meant staying in a hospital bed long enough for my vitals to stabilize. But as I found out through many cycles of treatment, that didn’t lead to me getting better.

To solve the national mental health crisis, we need an economic framework where doing good and doing good business are the same. By replacing the traditional model with outcome-based partnerships, we aren’t just building more efficient companies, but delivering on healthcare’s biggest promise: building a product that works.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.

title: AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
description:
As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.

title: The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness
description:
Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution

In Allen, a small town in Argentine Patagonia, many people living on the same street ended up falling ill. For some, it was severe migraines, nausea or skin irritation. For others, cancers, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages or stillbirth seemed to affect foetuses or children. People say it all started 13 years ago – when a well was drilled near their homes to extract gas and oil.

Calle Ciega 10 [Dead-end Street 10] lies on the eastern edge of Vaca Muerta, a vital area for Argentina’s economy, home to the world’s second-largest reserve of shale gas and fourth-largest reserve of shale oil. The region has more than 2,600 active wells, including one on this small street where about 20 families live, most of them seasonal workers on fruit farms.

title: Century-old Isle of Wight fossil reveals Europe's first megaraptoran
description:
Researchers have identified a new predatory dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, from a skull fragment found on the Isle of Wight, making it the first known megaraptoran found in Europe. The animal lived about 120 million years ago and was likely 3 to 4 metres long, with powerful forelimbs and curved claws estimated at 10 to 20 centimetres [sciencedaily.com#1][sci.news#1][cbsnews.com#2].

The Natural History Museum acquired the fossil in 1924, but it remained undescribed until a team led by University College London examined it. The discovery supports a proposed route in which megaraptorans spread from Asia through Europe to Gondwana, rather than reaching the southern continents by island-hopping. The researchers published the study in Royal Society Open Science on October 14, 2026 [sci.news#1][aawsat.com#1][sciencedaily.com#1].

title: Former ARPA-H director Renee Wegrzyn wants to solve science’s ‘magic hands’ problem
description:
Renee Wegrzyn spent her career building the future of American science—including the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, or ARPA-H, the White House agency created to accelerate health breakthroughs.

Then the Trump administration showed her the door. Wegrzyn cofounded Transfyr to tackle what she calls one of the most overlooked issues in science: the magic hands problem. She explains why fixing this unglamorous bottleneck is the prerequisite for everything AI promises to deliver in medicine, and why she can feel the next Sputnik moment coming—even if she can’t quite name it yet.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by Robert Safian, former editor-in-chief of Fast Company. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

You were at ARPA-H, the inaugural director of a White House effort to accelerate health research. You were amped up about the possibilities, but with the Trump administration, you had to pivot. Was it hard not to take it personally that they wanted different leadership?

I’ll tell you, I’m still amped up about it. It’s still an amazing idea. Obviously, DARPA [the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency] has been around for almost 80 years. I hope ARPA-H will have the same longevity and continue to live on today.

I’m a builder. I love to take things forward and really show what’s possible. So was it hard when I left? Of course it was hard. I had a really unusual appointment: I was a presidential appointee, but I was term-limited, so I served through the transition and had a few weeks in the new administration. I served in “Trump one,” by the way, as well.

So it was a great opportunity to make sure they really understood why we built the agency. We needed an ARPA-H because there was something missing in the way we were doing science broadly, which was: How do you move really quickly? How do you get focused on a problem versus building a general knowledge set? I was able to show them what we were building and convince them that it was worth keeping around. I couldn’t be more proud of the agency and its perseverance.

So your new business, Transfyr—The New York Times wrote about you, and the article kept referring to “magic hands.” I’m curious what magic hands are. What problem is Transfyr trying to solve or address?

You probably have your favorite dish, or your parents’ or grandparents’ favorite dish. Sometimes they just have the magic hands. Nobody can cook it like they do. Nobody can make it taste the special way they can. And that happens in science as well. There are some scientists who just have the knack and can deliver really great science over and over.

The challenge is that a lot of those scientists are such experts they can hardly describe what they’re doing. It’s an art in some ways. And so the magic hands idea was really a testament to what those scientists can do in the lab.

The pipeline we’re creating at Transfyr is: Can we create computer vision and perception tools to capture the work of science as it’s being done so that we understand, if the protocol says, “Mix the cells,” whether someone is inverting the tube in a certain gentle way, while another researcher may be rigorously shaking or vortexing it, which could destroy the sample?

Those little things, compounded over the many decisions a scientist may make over the course of several hours of experimentation, lead to what is called magic hands.

Was this an issue you saw at ARPA-H, the sort of breakthroughs that were trapped in a single lab in some ways?

Where that manifested at DARPA and at ARPA-H was in a realization, through my career, of how fragile breakthroughs are. Usually, the way a breakthrough is first communicated to the world is through a research publication, a Science or Nature paper. That paper is not a product. It’s not commercializable. It’s not ready for a patient that day. That’s the starting gun for what is going to happen.

The ARPAs of this world are really fantastic at getting to that initial breakthrough and demonstrating what is possible, but following through and delivering is not a 100% guaranteed activity.

When I started ARPA-H, we wanted customers, who would be the final users of that technology, to give us feedback on what we were developing so that when we got to the last day of the experiment, they were demanding that product, versus having that be the first contact with a customer, which unfortunately is pretty common around traditional grant-making organizations.

It’s rethinking how you make sure you can transfer that knowledge off the back end of a program.

Because the folks at the lab aren’t necessarily worrying about, or prioritizing, how to make it scalable. They’re just trying to see if it works. But of course, eventually we want it to be scalable.

Sometimes the folks in the lab don’t even have the expertise or understanding of who they need to talk to next to do that, right? We think about science and those transfers as handoffs. We deploy our technology to an originating lab to understand the science and what was important about that discovery, but we can also deploy it in a receiving lab so that we can see how they’re reproducing it.

And instead of the way we transfer science today, which is looking over each other’s shoulders and saying, “Oh, you’re doing it a little wrong,” we have this video-connectedness that lets us help accelerate those iterations of transferring the science.

Do you ever get frustrated about how resources are allocated in our world? You’ve put your life toward this work, and yet so much money is devoted to, I don’t know, space exploration or the next hot social app, the Meta Muse craze. How do you deal with government and how it prioritizes things?

Yeah, it’s maddening. One of the things that has me nervous right now is that I look back on the last 80 years following the Second World War. We’ve led the globe in science and engineering and innovation. Nobody who’s practicing science today has practiced science in the United States at a time when we weren’t, quote-unquote, winning from a competitiveness perspective, when we weren’t at the top.

I genuinely believe we may lose that competitiveness, that edge, that incumbency, and I’m not sure I see us fighting for it in the way that we should be. We have to deliver on what we’ve promised to do, and that’s a commitment not just to my country, but to my kids and my family. 

What I think a lot about is Sputnik moments. We’re going to look back at this moment in time like there’s something happening, and it’s going to impact whatever’s happening 20 to 50 years from now. You can feel it in the moment.

Where that happened before, of course, was Sputnik. The United States didn’t know the Soviet Union was developing that capability, and we didn’t have a counter-capability. What I realized is that each individual person has a Sputnik moment in their life that is usually health-related. My Sputnik moment was when my mother was diagnosed with cancer. That stopped everything.

Everybody has a story, whether it happened to them or their family, or if you talk to a member of Congress, something’s happening in their state that they can’t deal with.

So I’m like, “What is the Sputnik moment now?” If ARPA-H was bringing people from an unhealthy state to a healthy state, what’s happening now is taking us beyond that. If we can figure out and solve health and wellness, a lot of people talk about abundance. What is the next trajectory? What is the Sputnik that we’re working toward?

title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

title: From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
description:
Cultivating the nutritious bugs means families can raise livestock and enrich their own food, while lowering pressures on the land

A few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale feeds black soldier fly larvae to chickens in a coop above a fishpond. The larvae disappear in a scrum of chickens. Nearby, more larvae grow in modified jerrycans, while adult flies are kept in netted boxes.

Bikanyale kept chickens before he fled to Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But the cost of conventional feed and shortages of ingredients made them increasingly difficult to raise – a widespread pressure for millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.

Kanane Bikanyale tends to his black soldier fly larvae in a rearing unit in the Kyaka II refugee camp in Uganda

title: Learning Through Practice: Why Architecture Students Enter Competitions
description: On paper, entering an architecture competition is one of the most challenging things an architecture student can do. That distance from assessment is a relatively recent development, as competitions were once central to architectural education.

title: Brazil in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Housing, Learning Spaces, and Urban Life
description: This month's Brazil in Focus looks at how architecture and urban development intersect with questions of housing, education, public space, and mobility across the country. This month's selection includes an indigenous settlement in Maricá recognized by UN-Habitat for its approach to adequate housing, editorials examining university campuses and planned cities as frameworks for collective life, and projects ranging from a timber-structured airport expansion to a commercial building that engages São Paulo's public realm and a residence shaped by its landscape. Also on the radar are the winning proposal for Itaú Cultural's new headquarters on Avenida Paulista, international recognition for two Brazilian landscape architecture projects, and a national diagnosis highlighting persistent gaps in pedestrian infrastructure and road safety.
